title: Human-specific CCG-repeat insertion in the RBFOX1 promoter implicated in autism and speech enhances EGR1-responsive activity
authors: Lee, C.; Davenport, M. H.; Jarvis, E. D.
abstract: Human-specific promoter innovations have been predicted to shape human-specific traits. Here, we investigated the RBFOX1 splice regulator gene, which is specifically upregulated in human and songbird speech/song brain areas. We found that the human RBFOX1 promoter associated with autism and language impairment harbors a human-specific CCG trinucleotide insertion creating a functional CCG-repeat motif. Comparative single-nucleus transcriptome analyses of primate brains indicate that the human promoter drives differential expression in cortical excitatory neurons. Reporter assays show that the human CCG-repeat motif, relative to the chimpanzee allele, increases promoter activity with the EGR1 transcription factor. Genome-wide, the CCG-repeat motif marks core promoters of 104 genes, related to postsynaptic function and autism. In PTCHD1, a clinical duplication in autism patients creates another CCG-repeat motif that similarly increases EGR1-responsive promoter activity. Our findings suggest that small CCG-repeat variants in regulatory regions can exert large effects on gene regulation and apparent associated traits.

title: Pupil Dynamics Reflect Uncertainty-Driven Adjustments of Probability Learning
authors: Greenhouse-Tucknott, A.; Foucault, C.; Buot, A.; Meyniel, F.
abstract: Adaptive learning in dynamic environments depends on the brain's ability to represent and respond to uncertainty. Changes in arousal-mediated pupil diameter provide insight into the neural basis of this process. Prior work has focused on magnitude-based inference tasks and revealed that learning is primarily influenced by the detection of change points and the corresponding modulation of arousal. In comparison, the role of arousal systems in learning contexts where changes are harder to detect, such as in probability learning, remains poorly understood. Here, we combined pupillometry with a probability learning task in which human participants estimated a hidden generative probability of stimuli that changed abruptly and unpredictably. A Bayesian ideal observer model was used to estimate trial-by-trial learning rates and two uncertainty-associated factors: change point probability (the probability that the generative process has abruptly changed) and prior uncertainty (about the current beliefs on this generative process). In line with normative theory, participants relied on prior uncertainty to adjust learning rates. Pupil analyses revealed temporally distinct representations of uncertainty, with phasic dilations tracking change point probability and tonic pupil dilations tracking prior uncertainty. Mediation analyses further indicated that both phasic and tonic pupil signals partially carried the effects of change point probability and prior uncertainty on learning, respectively. Critically, high tonic arousal weakened the coupling between phasic pupil responses and change point probability, accompanied by a reduced influence of change point probability on learning. Together, our results demonstrate that probability learning in a dynamic environment is underpinned by computationally rational integration of latent uncertainty factors and its contribution to belief updating,regulated through arousal-associated responses.

title: Environmental co-option of chromatin potential links prenatal hypoxia to persistent cortical circuit dysfunction
authors: Cristancho, A. G.; Joseph, D. J.; Cassidy, M. M.; Chauhan, P. S.; Gadra, E. J.; Gadra, E. C.; Zarrinnegar, D.; Rodriguez, B. N.; Marsh, E. D.
abstract: Transient prenatal hypoxia is associated with long-term neurodevelopmental impairment without overt structural brain injury, suggesting early regulatory disruptions precede detectable pathology. Whether these disruptions represent transient stress responses or redirect developmental programs remains unknown. Here, we combined single-nucleus RNA sequencing and chromatin accessibility profiling in the late-gestation mouse cortex immediately after transient hypoxia, capturing responses across more than 140,000 nuclei. Hypoxia induced a largely conserved transcriptional stress response across cell types, whereas chromatin accessibility showed more extensive, cell type-specific disruption. Developing glutamatergic neurons showed the strongest disruption of chromatin transcription coupling, with hypoxia-responsive distal regulatory regions associated with genes governing synaptic organization and neuronal excitability. Consistent with these chromatin-associated programs, juvenile offspring displayed reduced dendritic spine density and increased intrinsic excitability in cortical neurons. These results support a model in which transient hypoxia co-opts the developing epigenome's capacity to encode future transcriptional states before persistent circuit dysfunction emerges.

title: AmyloCore-ML: AI/Machine Learning Enabled Identification of Amyloid Fibril Core Regions Using Protein Language Models
authors: Singh, J.; Jangid, R.; Srivastava, A.
abstract: Identification of amyloid forming regions in proteins remains central to understanding of their aggregation behaviour, which are central to various neurodegenerative and systemic disorders. Many predictors have been designed to identify amyloid forming regions, however they may not necessarily identify total residues found in actual disease associated fibril structures. To address this, we formed a sequence-based based predictor-AmyloCore-ML to ascertain structural amyloid-core propensity. The predictor was developed using experimentally determined fibril structures obtained from Amyloid Atlas. Ordered residues in the experimental structures were designated as core, and unresolved sampled from the same proteins as matched controls as non-core. Core and non-core regions were encoded using various physicochemical descriptors and protein language model (PLM) embeddings (ESM-2, ANKH, ProtT5) and evaluated using protein-grouped cross-validation. PLMs consistently outperformed physicochemical descriptors, with the best models reaching AUROC values of ~0.88 and AUPRC values of ~0.85. Locked full-length protein scans further localized experimental cores, with ESM-2/ExtraTrees achieving AUROC 0.833, AUPRC 0.751, and a mean peak distance of 12.4 residues. In comparative benchmarking, our predictor showed better performance metrics than CrossBeta and AggrescanAI. The framework therefore provides residue-resolved prediction of structurally incorporated amyloid-core regions directly from sequence.

title: MtbAIM: AI/ML-guided endpoint-specific prediction of small-molecule activity across drug-susceptible and drug-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis
abstract: The emergence of drug resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M.tb) presents a major challenge to drug discovery, as compounds active against drug-susceptible (DS) isolates may not retain comparable inhibitory activity against drug-resistant (DR) isolates. Here, we developed an AI/ML workflow to independently prioritize small molecules separately against DS and DR isolates of M.tb and predict MIC, MIC90, and MIC99 as distinct quantitative endpoints. Following curation of data retrieved from the ChEMBL repository, molecular-activity datasets comprised 25,645 and 3,749 compounds tested against whole cell DS and DR isolates respectively. Molecular representations were generated using RDKit descriptors and Morgan fingerprints, along with embeddings from ChemBERTa, MolCLR, and Uni-Mol, and evaluated for binary activity classification and endpoint-specific regression. The best-performing DS classifier combined RDKit/Morgan features with ExtraTrees (balanced accuracy 0.782; AUROC 0.864; AUPRC 0.870), while histogram gradient boosting using the same features performed best for DR classification (balanced accuracy 0.762; AUROC 0.836; AUPRC 0.880). Similarly, RDKit/Morgan features combined with tree-based regressors achieved the best overall performance across all six DS/DR regression endpoints, with pooled out-of-fold RMSE values ranging from 0.604 to 0.784 pMIC units. To facilitate broader application, we developed MtbAIM (https://github.com/jasdeep002/MtbAIM), a Google Colab-based prediction platform that enables users to assess and prioritize small molecules against DS and DR isolates of M.tb.

title: Computation or Weight Adaptation? Rethinking the Role of Plasticity in Learning
authors: Lior, G.; Shalev, Y.; Stanovsky, G.; Goldstein, A.
abstract: The human brain is an adaptive learning system that can generalize to new tasks and unfamiliar environments. The traditional view is that such adaptive behavior requires a structural change of the learning system (e.g., via neural plasticity). In this work, we use artificial neural networks, specifically large language models (LLMs), to challenge this traditional view and suggest that such adaptive behavior can be also achieved solely through computation if the learning system is sufficiently trained. We focus on statistical learning paradigms. These require identifying underlying regularities in seemingly arbitrary word sequences and are primarily considered to require neural plasticity. LLMs can capture arbitrary structures without requiring weight adaptation, despite divergence from their natural language training data. Our work provides novel insights into the role of plasticity in learning, demonstrating that sufficiently trained learning systems are highly flexible, adapting to new tasks and environments solely through computation, much more than previously acknowledged. Furthermore, our work opens the door for future research to use deep learning models to conjure hypotheses about the brain.

title: A critical evaluation of Gene Ontology priors in biologically-informed neural networks
authors: Verlaan, T.; Lieftinck, M.; Mwine, W.; Reinders, M.
abstract: Biologically-informed neural networks (BINNs) embed prior knowledge such as the Gene Ontology (GO) into their architecture to produce interpretable representations, yet whether and how this prior improves performance or interpretation remains unclear. We introduce GONNECT, a BINN incorporating GO into an autoencoder. We evaluate GO constraints in the encoder, decoder, or both on RNA-seq tumour samples from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), comparing against published BINNs (OntoVAE, VEGA), an unconstrained baseline, randomized priors, and untrained networks. Across various performance metrics, GO structure adds little to reconstruction or latent-space organization, frequently matched by randomized or unconstrained models. Node activations agree with a gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA)-derived reference, but this agreement largely arises from the architectural constraint: it is lost when GO connections are randomized, present even before training in the encoder, and learned in the decoder. Regularized soft links outside GO (GONNECT-SL) are unstable across runs and concentrate where the ontology is sparse, compensating for the prior's constraints rather than revealing new biology. Within this setting, we find no evidence that node activations capture biological information beyond that encoded by the predefined gene sets, suggesting that their apparent interpretability largely reflects the prior imposed by the architecture.

title: Histology-aware Inference of Cell-cell Communication in Spatial Transcriptomics
authors: Wang, X.; Tao, C.; Jiang, Y.; Jiang, Y.; Liu, H.; Jiang, Z.; Zhu, P.; Que, N.; Xi, J.; Price, S.; Qian, B.; Xu, J.; Li, C.
abstract: Cell-cell communication (CCC) is fundamental to tissue organization and function, yet inferring communication from spatial transcriptomics (ST) remains challenging because molecular and spatial information does not fully capture the anatomical context of signaling. Paired hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained images provide complementary insights into tissue architecture and cellular morphology, which remain underutilized as the explicit contextual constraint of CCC inference. Here we present HARMONIC, a histology-aware graph learning framework for anatomically contextualized CCC inference from ST and H&E images. HARMONIC uses conditional mutual information to model dependencies among tissue architecture, ligand-receptor-mediated signaling, gene expression and morphology, and integrates these representations through self-supervised graph learning. Across synthetic and biological datasets spanning platforms, species and tissues, HARMONIC suppresses less anatomically plausible interactions while recovering context-supported signaling across tumor-immune interfaces, necrotic transitions, anatomical compartments and microvascular structures. These findings establish tissue architecture as the explicit contextual constraint of spatial CCC inference.

title: 'broadSeq', a benchmarking tool to contrast differential gene expression methods and identify when genomic neighbourhood matters
authors: Das Roy, R.; Hallikas, O.; Kuure, S.; Jernvall, J.
abstract: Several tools are available to detect differential gene expression. The predominant approach of different statistical methods is to consider changes in gene expression independent from their genomic context. Previously, DELocal was introduced that takes into consideration gene expression dynamics in the genomic neighbourhood. Whereas DELocal was shown to identify developmentally regulated genes in developing mouse tooth, its performance in other biological conditions remains undetermined. To benchmark DElocal together with other methods, we develop another tool 'broadSeq'. It provides easy to use interface for methods like DELocal , deseq2, limma, edger, EBSeq and many more. Here we report benchmarking results on different data sets that comprise wild type developing mouse organs from different embryonic time points, and also human cancer data. The examined datasets are from the heart, kidney, liver, brain, forebrain, and hindbrain. We found that most methods produce relatively comparable lists of differentially expressed genes. Nevertheless, DELocal identifies partially distinct sets of genes compared to the other methods. Evaluating the identified genes using gene and disease ontology terms show that the uniquely detected genes by DELocal are biologically relevant and also highly expressed compared to the genes identified by the other methods. Because consistently highly expressed genes show relatively subtle fold changes, the neighbourhood concept of DELocal appears to correct for the difficulty in detecting these differential expression of highly expressed genes. Finally, we provide the tools as combined bioconductor packages, allowing researchers to explore and decide the best methods for their data and questions.

title: Cell Painting and machine learning for mechanistic profiling of hepatotoxic botanicals and their constituents
authors: Ollitrault, G.; Mitchell, C. A.; Ferguson, S. S.; Roe, A. L.; White, B.; Titterton, K.; Ewald, J.
abstract: BACKGROUND Botanicals are widely consumed as herbal remedies and plant-derived products, but their complex and variable chemical composition presents major challenges for safety assessment. Although hepatotoxicity has been reported for several botanicals, the constituent compounds responsible and the underlying mechanisms often remain poorly characterised. OBJECTIVES We aimed to determine whether Cell Painting could identify candidate constituent drivers of botanical bioactivity and generate hypotheses about potential mechanisms of action in primary human hepatocytes. METHODS We profiled 13 botanical extracts and 85 known constituents across multiple concentrations using Cell Painting alongside assays of metabolic activity and membrane integrity. To interpret morphological phenotypes, we trained machine-learning models using a Cell Painting reference atlas of >1,000 chemicals linked to ToxCast/Tox21 molecular and cellular bioactivity annotations. RESULTS Cell Painting detected bioactivity in 11/13 botanical extracts and 46/85 constituents, compared with 9/13 extracts and 40/85 constituents in the cell-health assays, and generally detected activity at lower concentrations. For 9/13 extracts, at least one constituent was active at a lower concentration than the corresponding botanical extract, supporting the contribution of a subset of potent constituents to mixture-level responses. Aristolochia and goldenseal were the most potent extracts across Cell Painting and cell-health assays and contained highly active constituents. Reference-atlas models generated specific mechanistic hypotheses, including cytotoxicity-, endocrine-, and genotoxicity-associated responses for several botanicals and constituents. CONCLUSION These results support Cell Painting combined with machine learning as a sensitive approach for characterising cellular responses to botanicals, prioritising candidate constituent drivers of hepatotoxicity-associated phenotypes, and generating testable hypotheses about potential mechanisms of action.

title: CLEAR-FORCE: A reservoir computing framework for closed-loop brain stimulation
authors: Moreno-Gris, A.; Godin, C.; Thivierge, J.-P.
abstract: Electrical stimulation of brain activity has emerged as a key therapeutic intervention for neurological diseases. The success of these approaches relies on precisely tuned stimulation parameters. A major challenge is that these parameters should ideally be adjusted in real-time based on changes in brain activity. Closed-loop controllers address this challenge by monitoring brain activity and adapting stimulation according to ongoing changes in neural dynamics. While machine learning has been helpful in this context, closed-loop controllers typically do not adapt in real-time to fluctuations in brain activity. Here, we propose a novel framework based on reservoir computing to train a closed-loop, real-time neural controller. This approach, termed CLEAR-FORCE, trains the output weights of a recurrent network based on a combination of target signals and feedback from brain activity. Two series of simulations were performed, where the controller was successful at (1) inducing neural oscillations in a population of spiking neurons and (2) suppressing pathological oscillations. This framework provides a promising avenue for the implementation of neural controllers in low-powered, real-time, and adaptive hardware that harnesses machine learning for the personalized treatment of brain disorders.

title: Impaired Control Symptoms in Alcohol Use Disorder Show Convergent Associations Across Behavioral and Neural Markers of Inhibitory Control and Drinking Behavior
authors: Boehmer, J.; Reinhardt, P.; Bottino, M.; Baertl, C.; Arntz, F.; Hildebrandt, M. K.; Chen, H.; Thill, L.; Petzold, J.; Ritter, K.; Rapp, M.; Kiefer, F.; Bach, P.; Lenz, B.; Heinz, A.; Spitta, G.; Rosenthal, A.; Endrass, T.; Smolka, M. N.; Spanagel, R.; Henze, G.-I.; ReCoDe-Consortium,  ; Marxen, M.; Walter, H.
abstract: Background: Deficits in inhibitory control are considered a central feature of alcohol use disorder (AUD), yet behavioral and neuroimaging findings have been inconsistent. One potential explanation is the marked heterogeneity of AUD, which encompasses multiple symptom dimensions that may differ in their underlying neurocognitive mechanisms. In this study, we investigated whether behavioral and neural markers of inhibitory control are associated with specific DSM-5 AUD symptom domains. Methods: A total of 589 participants (432 with non-treatment seeking AUD, 157 controls) completed a Stop-Signal Task (SST) during fMRI. Associations between DSM-5 symptom domains (impaired control over alcohol use, risky use, social problems, physical dependence) and SST performance, inhibition-related brain activation, and alcohol consumption were examined. Real-life drinking behavior was additionally assessed over 12 months using ecological momentary assessment (EMA). Results: Greater impaired control symptom severity was associated with poorer performance on go trials and diminished post-error slowing during SST. At the neural level, higher impaired control symptom severity was associated with reduced activation across fronto-insular, parietal, cingulate, supplementary motor, and cerebellar regions. In contrast, other symptom domains showed little to no associations with inhibition-related behavioral or neural measures. Higher impaired control symptom severity was associated with greater alcohol consumption across questionnaire-based and EMA-based assessments. Conclusions: In this large cohort, altered behavioral performance and recruitment of inhibition-related brain regions in the SST was selectively linked to impaired control symptoms. These findings highlight the importance of symptom-based approaches for understanding heterogeneity in addiction and may inform the development of more targeted interventions.

title: Cerebral hemodynamics and cytochrome c oxidase in hypoxic-ischemic rabbit fetuses
authors: Cortese, L.; Lo Presti, G.; Berdun, S.; Bale, G.; Kovacsova, Z.; Eixarch, E.; Gratacos, E.; Tachtsidis, I.; Durduran, T.
abstract: Background: Understanding fetal brain responses to hypoxia-ischemia is of growing interest, as it remains unclear to what extent these responses differ from those of newborns and whether developmental adaptations during gestation contribute to such differences. Materials and methods: Using a combination of broadband near-infrared spectroscopy (bNIRS) and diffuse correlation spectroscopy (DCS), we measured brain microvascular oxygen saturation (StO2), total hemoglobin concentration (THC), relative cerebral blood flow (rCBF), and the oxidation state of cytochrome c oxidase (oxCCO) during an acute ischemic challenge in the brains of five rabbit fetuses in utero. Simultaneous measurements were acquired from four control fetuses located in the contralateral uterine horn. Results: During the hypoxia-ischemia phase, we observed a rapid reduction of CBF (47% +/- 29%) and StO2, (from 64.7% +/- 1.5% at baseline to 40.6% +/- 2.0%) together with an increase of oxCCO (3.7 uM +/- 0.5 uM). Conclusion: The simultaneous increase in oxCCO and decrease in rCBF and StO2 during hypoxia-ischemia reveals a cerebral response pattern that differs from that commonly reported in the newborn brain. These findings support the hypothesis that unique developmental adaptations influence fetal cerebral metabolism during hypoxic-ischemic stress.

title: Default Mode Network Connectivity Is Associated with Capture by Distractors Assigned to Learned Spatial Regularities
authors: Chen, S.; Mueller, H. J.; Shi, Z.
abstract: Salient distractors interfere with visual search, but observers can learn to filter out distractors that occur frequently and in predictable locations. We examined whether within-default-mode-network (DMN) task-run connectivity was associated with distractor capture and its location-dependent modulation in task-fMRI data from two groups in which either orientation or color distractors carried a spatial-probability bias. Higher within-DMN connectivity was associated with greater distractor capture by the biased distractor dimension, which was also the most frequent distractor type, whereas capture by the unbiased dimension was essentially unrelated to connectivity. A hierarchical trial-level model also showed stronger DMN-distractor-capture coupling for the biased than for the unbiased dimension when both were evaluated under the same frequent-/rare-region weighting. DMN connectivity was also associated with spatial-probability learning, indexed by the rare-minus-frequent reaction-time difference on biased-dimension trials, but this association was closely tied to overall capture. When the physical distractor dimension was held constant, orientation showed stronger DMN-distractor-capture coupling when it carried the spatial bias; in contrast, the corresponding color comparison remained uncertain. The broader network analyses provided converging support for this DMN-distractor-capture coupling pattern. Higher DMN connectivity was thus not associated with poorer performance in general, but with less effective filtering of the distractor that the task set was tuned to suppress. This pattern is consistent with a DMN state that interferes with implementing the optimal task set.
